ety.text: From Middle English cost, from Old English cost (“option, choice, possibility, manner, way, condition”), from Old Norse kostr (“choice, opportunity, chance, condition, state, quality”), from Proto-Germanic *kustuz (“choice, trial”) (or Proto-Germanic *kustiz (“choice, trial”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus (“to enjoy, taste”).

senses.d: To incur a charge of; to require payment of a (specified) price.
ex: This shirt cost $50, while this was cheaper at only $30.
It will cost you a lot of money to take a trip around the world.

senses.d: To cause something to be lost; to cause the expenditure or relinquishment of.
ex: Trying to rescue the man from the burning building cost them their lives.
though it cost me ten nights' watchings

senses.d: To require to be borne or suffered; to cause.
ex: to do him wanton rites, which cost them woe
LUKE: "That little droid is going to cost me a lot of trouble."

senses.d: To calculate or estimate a price.
ex: I'd cost the repair work at a few thousand.

senses.d: To cost (a person) a great deal of money or suffering.
ex: I can give you the names, but it'll cost you.

senses.d: Amount of money, time, etc. that is required or used.

senses.d: A negative consequence or loss that occurs or is required to occur.
ex: Spending all your time working may earn you a lot of money at the cost of your health.
